pages.title: Welcome to Videolab
pages.body:
Videolab lets you see, and change, the technical properties of a digital video image while it plays. Six labs each simulate one concept:

  • Resolution: how many pixels make up the picture;
  • Frame rate: how many pictures are taken each second;
  • Aspect ratio and anamorphic formats: the shape of the picture;
  • Interlaced scanning: lines, fields and combing;
  • Chroma sampling: luminance, chrominance and subsampling;
  • Colour depth: bits per channel and banding.

Every lab works on the built-in test signal, on your webcam, or on any video or image you open.

pages.title: Choose a signal
pages.body:
LIVE uses your webcam; the browser will ask for permission. LOAD FILE opens a video or image from your computer. You can also drop a file onto the deck. Files stay on your computer.

TEST SIGNAL plays Videolab's test card, designed to show every effect: the circle and squares (aspect), the gradients (colour depth), the coloured lettering (chroma), the fine lines (resolution and interlace), and the moving ball and wheel (motion).

pages.title: Transport and display
pages.body:
STILL freezes the picture. The two SPEED keys slow playback down to 1/16 or speed it up to ×2. Slow motion makes frames and fields much easier to see.

The display shows the time code (hours:minutes:seconds:frames) and the current settings.

pages.title: Lab modes
pages.body:
Choose one of the six labs. Its controls appear on the panel below. The first time you open a lab, a short tutorial explains the concept. Press ? at any time to read it again.

Press the lit lab key again to switch the lab off and see the untouched signal.

pages.title: Looking closer
pages.body:
ZOOM magnifies the picture from ×2 to ×16. Click the screen to choose where to look, and drag to move around. Double-click toggles a ×4 zoom; the mouse wheel also zooms. From about ×8 a grid outlines each pixel.

4:3 / 16:9 changes the shape of the monitor. SNAP saves the picture, OSD hides the on-screen text, and LANGUAGE switches between English and Portuguese.

Videolab was created by Eduardo Morais in 2013 as a Processing application for teaching digital video. This web edition rebuilds it for the browser.

pages.title: Pixels and lines
pages.body:
A digital picture is a grid of pixels (picture elements). Each pixel holds one colour value. Its resolution is the number of pixels across times the number of lines down, for example 1920 × 1080.

Any detail smaller than a pixel cannot be recorded. In video, formats are often named by their number of lines: 576, 720, 1080, 2160.

pages.title: Common formats
pages.body:
SD: 720 × 576 (PAL, Europe) or 720 × 480 (NTSC), used by DV, DVCAM and DVD. HD: 1280 × 720. Full HD: 1920 × 1080. UHD: 3840 × 2160, sold as “4K” television; cinema 4K (DCI) is 4096 × 2160.

Doubling the number of lines multiplies the number of pixels by four: Full HD has about 2.1 million pixels, UHD about 8.3 million.

pages.title: Resolution is not sharpness
pages.body:
Resolution is the capacity to record detail. The detail you really get also depends on the lens, focus, movement and compression.

Enlarging a picture never adds detail: the scaler only estimates the missing values. Nearest neighbour repeats each pixel and shows blocks. Bilinear blends neighbours and looks soft.

If your webcam delivers 640 × 480, choosing 2160 lines will not improve it. The screen shows UPSCALED when this happens. Your own monitor also has a limited number of pixels: use ZOOM to see the finest rasters.

pages.title: Try it
pages.body:
Lower the number of lines and watch the vertical bars in the middle of the test card. When the raster cannot reproduce them, the bars turn grey or form false patterns: this is aliasing (moiré).

Compare the two scalers, then use ZOOM ×8 or more to see the pixel grid.

pages.title: Pictures per second
pages.body:
Video, like film, is a sequence of still pictures shown in quick succession. Our perception fuses them into continuous movement.

The number of pictures per second is the frame rate, measured in frames per second (fps). A higher rate samples movement more often, so motion looks smoother, but it needs more data.

pages.title: Standard rates
pages.body:
24 fps: cinema, since sound film in the late 1920s. 25 fps: PAL and SECAM television (Europe), tied to the 50 Hz power grid. 30 fps (precisely 29.97): NTSC television (Americas, Japan), tied to 60 Hz. 50 and 60 fps: sport, live television and games.

The 29.97 rate dates from the introduction of NTSC colour in 1953, which slowed 30 fps by 0.1 %.

pages.title: Shutter and motion blur
pages.body:
Each frame is exposed for only part of its interval. Film cameras used a rotating disc, so exposure is still described as a shutter angle: 360° exposes the whole interval, 180° half of it.

The classic choice is 180°, an exposure of 1/(2 × fps): 1/50 s at 25 fps. Longer exposures blur moving objects. Shorter ones give sharp frames, but movement looks jerky and stroboscopic.

pages.title: Temporal aliasing
pages.body:
A repeating movement close to the frame rate can seem to stop or run backwards. This is the wagon-wheel effect.

The wheel on the test card has 12 spokes and turns twice per second, so its pattern repeats 24 times per second. At 24 fps it seems frozen; at 25 fps it drifts backwards. The red spoke shows the real rotation.

pages.title: Try it
pages.body:
Change the frame rate and the shutter angle while you watch the ball and the wheel.

Most screens refresh 60 times per second. Rates that do not divide 60 exactly (50, 25, 24) are shown with uneven repetitions, a stutter called judder. Television had the same problem when showing 24 fps films at 60 Hz, solved with the 3:2 pulldown.

pages.title: The shape of the picture
pages.body:
The aspect ratio is the proportion between the width and the height of the picture. It is written as a ratio, 4:3, or as a decimal, 1.33:1.

The most common ratios in video are 4:3, called standard, and 16:9, called widescreen. Cinema also uses 1.85:1 and 2.39:1 (“scope”).

pages.title: From 4:3 to 16:9
pages.body:
4:3 (1.33) was close to the shape of cinema until the 1950s and was the shape of television for most of its history. When television spread, cinema answered with much wider formats.

16:9 (1.78) was proposed in the 1980s as a compromise: 4:3 and 2.39 both fit into it with similar black bars. It became the standard for HD and almost every screen sold today.

pages.title: Different shapes on one screen
pages.body:
When the picture and the screen have different shapes, there are three choices:

  • Box: show the whole picture and add black bars, above and below (letterbox) or at the sides (pillarbox);
  • Crop: fill the screen and lose part of the picture (pan & scan);
  • Stretch: fill the screen by distorting the picture, so circles become ellipses.

pages.title: Anamorphic formats
pages.body:
An anamorphic format records a wide picture squeezed into a narrower frame, and the display stretches it back.

CinemaScope lenses squeezed the picture by 2× onto 35 mm film. SD video does the same: DV, DVCAM and DVD record 16:9 in the same 720 × 576 frame as 4:3, and a signal tells the television to unsqueeze it. If the display ignores it, people look too tall and thin.

pages.title: Pixel aspect ratio
pages.body:
Because of anamorphic recording, SD pixels are not square. The shape on screen depends on the number of pixels and on their shape:

DISPLAY ASPECT = (WIDTH ÷ HEIGHT) × PIXEL ASPECT

HD, UHD and computer images use square pixels (1:1). Editing software must know the pixel aspect of SD footage, or it will show it distorted.

pages.title: Try it
pages.body:
Change the shape of the picture and of the monitor, then compare box, crop and stretch. On the test card, the circle must stay round and the grid squares must stay square.

Choose a 16:9 picture and press SQUEEZE: the inset shows what is recorded on tape. Switch UNSQUEEZE off to see the picture on a monitor that ignores the anamorphic signal.

pages.title: Scanning the picture
pages.body:
A cathode-ray tube (CRT) television draws the picture with an electron beam, line by line, from top to bottom. It fills the screen in a fraction of a second.

The first television systems, in the 1930s, could not transmit enough lines 50 times per second. The solution was to scan the picture in an interlaced way.

pages.title: Progressive video
pages.body:
In progressive video each frame is complete: all its lines show the same instant, like a frame of film.

At 25 progressive frames per second (25p), pictures are taken 40 ms apart (1 s ÷ 25).

pages.title: Interlaced video
pages.body:
In interlaced video each picture is divided into two fields: one with the odd lines, one with the even lines. The fields are captured one after the other.

At 50 fields per second (50i), each field is captured 20 ms after the previous one. The two fields of one frame show two different instants. Motion is sampled 50 times per second, but each sample has only half the lines.

pages.title: Combing and deinterlacing
pages.body:
A CRT shows the fields one after the other. Flat screens and computers show whole frames, so the two fields are woven together and moving edges show teeth: combing.

Deinterlacing converts fields to frames: weave joins two fields (sharp, but combs on motion); bob stretches each field to full height (smooth, but softer and with flickering edges). Fine horizontal lines also flicker on interlaced displays, an effect called twitter.

pages.title: Format names
pages.body:
The letter after the number of lines tells the scanning: 576i (PAL SD, used by DV and DVCAM), 480i (NTSC SD), 1080i (broadcast HD), 720p and 1080p.

The number after the letter is written in different ways. 1080i50 and 1080i/25 describe the same signal: 50 fields, or 25 frames, per second.

pages.title: Try it
pages.body:
Compare PROG and INTER while the ball moves. FIELD shows one field at a time, as a CRT would; BOB shows a line-doubled field.

Slow playback down to 1/16 to see the two fields alternate. LINE SIZE makes each line thicker, so the structure is easier to see.

pages.title: Luminance and chrominance
pages.body:
When colour television arrived (NTSC in 1953, PAL and SECAM in the 1960s), the signal had to stay compatible with black-and-white sets.

The solution was component video: send the brightness information, the luminance, as before, and add two colour channels, the chrominance. Black-and-white sets ignore the chrominance; colour sets rebuild the RGB picture from all three.

pages.title: From RGB to Y′CbCr
pages.body:
Cameras and screens work in RGB, but most video formats store luminance and chrominance. Luminance (Y′) is a weighted sum of the three primaries:

Y′ = 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B

The two chrominance channels are colour differences: Cb is based on B − Y′ and Cr on R − Y′. Together they are called Y′CbCr in digital video, often shortened to YUV.

These weights come from SD (BT.601); HD (BT.709) uses slightly different ones.

pages.title: Sampling
pages.body:
Our vision is more sensitive to fine detail in brightness than to fine detail in colour.

To save data, most video formats record chrominance at a lower resolution than luminance. This is chroma subsampling. The loss is hard to see in natural pictures.

pages.title: Types of subsampling
pages.body:
The notation describes a block 4 pixels wide and 2 lines high:

  • 4:4:4: every pixel has its own chrominance (no subsampling);
  • 4:2:2: two pixels side by side share it (professional formats, broadcast);
  • 4:2:0: a 2 × 2 square of pixels shares it (DV and DVCAM in PAL, DVD, Blu-ray, streaming);
  • 4:1:1: four pixels in a row share it (DV and DVCAM in NTSC).

pages.title: Where it shows
pages.body:
Subsampling shows at sharp edges between strong colours, such as red titles on blue. It also matters for chroma keying (green screen), where the colour edge defines the mask, and in colour grading.

Each new compression with subsampling can soften colour edges further.

pages.title: Try it
pages.body:
Switch luminance (Y) and chrominance (CbCr) on and off. With Y only you see a black-and-white television picture. With CbCr only you see how little detail colour carries.

Then try the different subsampling types on the coloured lettering of the test card.

pages.title: Make it obvious
pages.body:
EXAGGERATE enlarges the chroma blocks so the effect is visible at a glance. At ×1 the simulation is true to scale.

Use ZOOM on a coloured edge to see the real blocks pixel by pixel.

pages.title: Bits per channel
pages.body:
Colour depth is the number of bits used for each channel (R, G, B or Y′, Cb, Cr) of every pixel. It sets how many values the channel can take:

LEVELS = 2BITS

With 4 bits per channel, each primary has 16 levels, so a pixel can take 16 × 16 × 16 = 4096 colours.

pages.title: 8 bits and beyond
pages.body:
With 8 bits per channel, each primary has 256 levels: more than 16.7 million colours. This roughly matches what we can tell apart, and most delivery formats use it.

But 8 bits leave little room for colour and contrast changes in post-production. Professional formats and HDR use 10 bits (1024 levels) or 12 bits (4096 levels).

Video often keeps luminance between 16 and 235, so 8-bit video has only 220 levels of brightness.

pages.title: Banding and dithering
pages.body:
With too few levels, smooth gradients such as skies or vignettes show visible steps: banding, also called posterisation. It gets worse when contrast is pushed in grading.

Dithering adds a fine pattern of noise before rounding. The steps break up and the eye averages them into a smoother gradient.

pages.title: Try it
pages.body:
Lower the number of bits and watch the gradients and the sky. GRADIENT places a chart of ramps over the picture; DITHER applies an ordered 4 × 4 dither.

Most screens show 8 bits per channel, so depths above 8 cannot be simulated. The low depths show the kind of banding that appears when 8-bit footage is graded.
